summary: Describes HOTP, an algorithm that turns a shared secret and a counter into one-time passwords using HMAC. It includes a security analysis and guidance on deploying it safely. It can be used in many places, from VPN logins to Wi-Fi sign-in and web transactions, and was written to encourage interoperable two-factor authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: You and a website share a secret recipe and both count the same number. Each time you cook, you get a new code that works only once, so a stolen old code is useless.

subtitle: How a shared secret and a counter become a short code that works only once.

tldr.problem: Two-factor authentication was held back by proprietary tokens that did not work with each other, and static passwords were proving inadequate.
tldr.mechanism: The token and the server share a secret key K and an 8-byte counter C. Each code is HMAC-SHA-1(K,C), cut down by dynamic truncation to a short number of at least 6 digits.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives an open, freely implementable algorithm, plus rules for throttling, counter resynchronization and secret handling. Its security analysis concludes that the best attack is brute force.

today: RFC 4226 is an Informational RFC. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text itself does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why an Open One-Time Password
sections.content:
The RFC argues that two-factor authentication was rare because vendors' hardware and software were tied together by proprietary technology. That meant high costs, poor adoption and little innovation. Static passwords were also showing their weakness against rising network threats.

The authors, members of the Open AuTHentication (OATH) initiative, propose a simple algorithm that any manufacturer or developer can implement. It is event-based, so it fits high-volume devices such as Java smart cards, USB dongles and GSM SIM cards. It is made freely available under the IETF rules of RFC 3979.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone used their own secret lock that only fit their own key. This memo offers one shared lock design that anybody can build.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
Six requirements, R1 to R6, drove the design:

  • R1: the algorithm MUST be sequence- or counter-based.
  • R2: it SHOULD be cheap to implement in hardware (battery, buttons, processing power, display size).
  • R3: it MUST work with tokens that have no numeric input.
  • R4: the displayed value MUST be easy to read and enter, so it must be at least 6 digits and preferably numeric only.
  • R5: there MUST be user-friendly ways to resynchronize the counter.
  • R6: it MUST use a strong shared secret of at least 128 bits. 160 bits is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The code has to be short enough to type, cheap enough for a tiny gadget, and the secret has to be long enough that nobody can guess it.

sections.title: Computing an HOTP Value
sections.content:
The formula is HOTP(K,C) = Truncate(HMAC-SHA-1(K,C)). K is the secret shared by client and server, and C is an 8-byte counter, the moving factor, which MUST be synchronized between them. HMAC is defined in RFC 2104.

The HMAC-SHA-1 result is 20 bytes (160 bits), too long to type. Dynamic truncation shrinks it in three steps:

  • Take the low-order 4 bits of the last byte (byte 19) as an offset from 0 to 15.
  • Read the 4 bytes starting at that offset and mask the top bit, giving a 31-bit number. This avoids confusion between signed and unsigned arithmetic.
  • Compute that number modulo 10^Digit.

Implementations MUST be able to produce a 6-digit code at a minimum and possibly 7 or 8 digits. The RFC's worked example has an offset of 10 (0xa), four bytes 0x50ef7f19 and the result 872921.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret and the count are mixed into a long scrambled number. A rule that depends on the number itself picks a small piece, and that piece becomes your short code.

sections.title: Server Checks, Throttling and Resynchronization
sections.content:
The token increments its counter each time the user asks for a new code. The server increments its counter only after a successful validation, so the two can drift apart. To cope, the server sets a look-ahead window s and tries the next s counter values. It MAY ask the user for a short sequence of codes (say 2 or 3), since forging consecutive values is harder. s SHOULD be as low as usability allows.

Because the code is short, brute force is possible, so the server RECOMMENDs a throttling parameter T, the maximum number of attempts. An alternative is an increasing delay of T*A seconds after the A-th failure. Delay or lockout schemes MUST apply across login sessions so parallel guessing does not get around them. When the maximum is reached, the server SHOULD lock the account and tell the user.

The protocol around HOTP must support two-factor authentication (RP1), SHOULD resist brute force (RP2) and SHOULD run over a secure channel (RP3). HOTP is not a substitute for encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: If your counter runs ahead because you pressed the button a few extra times, the website peeks a few numbers ahead to catch up. It also locks the door after too many wrong guesses.

sections.title: Security Analysis and Secret Management
sections.content:
Appendix A analyses HOTP and concludes that, for practical purposes, truncated outputs for different counters behave like independent, uniform 31-bit strings. Reducing modulo 10^Digit adds only a negligible bias, so the best possible attack is brute force. The RFC approximates the attacker's success probability as Sec = sv/10^Digit, where s is the look-ahead window, v the number of verification attempts and Digit the code length. Appendix B argues that the 2005 attacks on SHA-1 do not affect HMAC-SHA-1 or HOTP.

For secrets, the RFC describes two approaches. With deterministic generation, secrets are derived from a master key that MUST be kept in a tamper-resistant device. With random generation, secrets are made from a good random source (see RFC 4086) and stored encrypted in a secure area. Section 8 adds optional composite secrets that mix in a PIN or other factor held at the token.
sections.plainLanguage: Smart people checked and found the only way to cheat is to keep guessing, so the answer is to limit guesses and keep the secret locked away.

sections.title: Optional Extensions
sections.content:
Appendix E lists variations that are not part of the standard algorithm:

  • More digits, such as 8, which lowers the attacker's chance from sv/10^6 to sv/10^8.
  • A subset of 32 alphanumeric symbols instead of digits.
  • Asking for a sequence of L codes, with L defaulting to 1.
  • A counter-based resynchronization protocol where the client also sends its counter, so no look-ahead window is needed. The RFC says it SHOULD be used when its impact is acceptable.
  • An optional Data field, including a time-based value as a moving factor.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want a stronger lock, you can use a longer code, letters as well as numbers, or ask for several codes in a row.
